calibration.reference_10: Seeing Theory, Brown University (seeing-theory.brown.edu) — its Regression and Sampling Distributions chapters: you drag points and watch r respond, and one control draws hundreds of samples so the law of large numbers is witnessed, not inferred.
calibration.reference_8: BBC Bitesize GCSE Maths interactive guides (e.g. 'Analysing data') with GOV.UK-level accessibility — assignable tomorrow unedited, every control labelled, focus authored, contrast verified.

verdict: Both R3 blockers are resolved with the requested code — chip and step-pill boundaries now sit at 3.86:1 and 5.9:1 (styles.css:94, 64) with both ratios in TEST_REPORT.md:75, and Reset uses the confirm-in-place pattern with a live announcement (app.js:107-119). This is Bitesize-level copy with authored, verified accessibility: every chart has a description and a labelled scrollable table, focus is authored and inverts in the dark header, targets are 44px, reduced motion is honoured, and the lesson runs one-handed at 360px. It lands on the 8 rung; the residuals (one-tap notebook clear, unexplained disabled Next, the mobile notebook below a 3,000px card) are refinements, not obstacles to assigning it tomorrow.

The three experiment gates that refuse to grade until the learner has manipulated something: 'Run the experiment first.' (app.js:191), 'Draw first, then decide.' (app.js:288), 'Look inside the seasons first.' (app.js:346).

Feedback that names the misconception instead of right/wrong — 'Bigger samples are less noisy… The convenience sample's problem isn't noise, it's who gets picked.' (app.js:294) and 'The zoomed view didn't invent a difference; it magnified a real, small one.' (app.js:196).

The chart package on all three charts: role=img with aria-labelledby caption and description, axis titles with units, text legends, and a labelled scrollable data table (index.html:67-72, index.html:159-161, index.html:196-210; tables built at app.js:174-177, app.js:262-267, app.js:330-333).

The no-pressure stance at ladder level: 'nothing is scored against you' (index.html:52), 'Not yet — have another look.' / 'Almost.' feedback labels, unlimited retry, no attempt counter and no timer anywhere in the lesson.
gap_to_10: Seeing Theory, Brown University (seeing-theory.brown.edu): its Sampling Distributions chapter lets one gesture draw hundreds of samples, so the learner watches the random cloud tighten on the truth while the biased cloud stays put — here draws must be pressed one at a time, so the law of large numbers is inferred from a strip of dots rather than witnessed. Its Regression chapter also lets the learner drag individual points and see r respond live; this build's vocabulary is slider, button and checkbox — precise, but never that single tactile aha.
